title: Noninvasive cellular-resolution read and write through the intact adult human skull

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a way to observe individual neurons and selectively change their activity in an awake adult human without opening, replacing or implanting devices through the skull. Its read mode would distinguish the timing of spikes from many individually tracked neurons, including neurons at depth. Its write mode would alter the activity of a chosen neuron or a precisely defined small group. These are two distinct capabilities: successfully recording cellular activity would not, by itself, demonstrate selective stimulation.

Cellular resolution here means distinguishing individual neurons and their electrical activity, rather than producing an image with small pixels or detecting a local change in blood flow. A hemodynamic signal can carry useful information about brain activity without resolving individual spikes. Likewise, successful behavior or language decoding does not establish that the underlying measurement identifies individual neurons. The supplied fMRI and implanted inner-speech studies illustrate these different levels of access.

The central challenge is physical access through the intact adult skull, coupled with reliable identification and targeting of cells. A 2025 perspective documents substantial skull-related obstacles to light- and sound-based imaging, including distortions of waves passing through bone. That establishes an important barrier, but neither an absolute prohibition on cellular access nor proof that every possible recording and stimulation approach has failed.

significance.text: Conditional synthesis: stable cellular readout and selective perturbation without cranial surgery would give human neuroscience a powerful new form of experimental access. Researchers could relate the activity of identified neurons to ongoing behavior, then test causal hypotheses by changing selected cells and observing the consequences. The direct advance would be access to human cellular circuits without surgical entry; its value would depend on the number of accessible neurons, their depth, recording stability and perturbation specificity.

The supplied evidence illustrates why this would be a major advance. Tang and colleagues demonstrated noninvasive reconstruction of language meaning from hemodynamic fMRI signals, while Kunz and colleagues studied inner speech using implanted intracortical microelectrode arrays. Overcoming skull-related imaging barriers while retaining cellular specificity could bridge important parts of that access gap. These examples do not establish an exhaustive division in which every noninvasive technique is coarse and every invasive technique is local.

Conditional synthesis: the capability could support longitudinal studies of learning and disease and provide a platform for future circuit-directed treatments. Routine clinical use would require additional evidence about coverage, targeting, repeated-session safety, clinical benefit, cost and deployment. A successful laboratory demonstration would not make cellular neuroscience or effective treatment as accessible as an ordinary scan.

Physical access would also leave interpretation unsolved. A universal interface for unspoken thought would require reliable mappings between neural activity and mental content, generalization beyond trained tasks, and validation across people and contexts. The 2025 implanted inner-speech study explicitly reports that accurate decoding of complete, intelligible sentences during free-form thinking was not possible. That limitation constrains extrapolation from demonstrated decoding; it does not rule out future advances.

Physical feasibility remains uncertain. The documented transcranial propagation problem motivates that uncertainty, but the supplied perspective does not establish an ultimate single-neuron resolution ceiling. The research notes' assumption of a long development timeline is not an evidence-based forecast; the supplied material supports neither a reliable completion date nor a conclusion of permanent impossibility.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing physical capability is transmission and recovery of sufficiently specific information through adult skull while preserving useful access to the brain beneath it. For light- and sound-based approaches, the supplied perspective identifies skull-induced wave distortions and efforts to characterize, model and compensate for them. Its retained abstract supports the importance of this engineering problem without establishing which compensation strategy could reach cellular resolution.

Engineering synthesis: a read system would need to separate overlapping contributions from nearby active cells, distinguish neural signals from motion and other interference, recover spike timing, and maintain cell identity across time. It would also need to show that apparent cellular signals are not reconstructions driven mainly by assumptions or correlations with behavior. The earlier notes invoke the electromagnetic inverse problem and limitations of scalp measurements, but the supplied review does not substantiate those modality-specific claims sufficiently to treat them as established explanations here.

Engineering synthesis: selective write requires a separate solution to targeting. A system must change the intended cell or small group while measuring effects on neighboring cells and more distant circuits. A focal-looking stimulus or a behavioral response would not alone demonstrate cellular selectivity. Any proposed approach must also explain how targets are identified and reached without surgery or a required implanted interface.

Engineering synthesis: these capabilities must coexist at useful depth, over a meaningful field of view and for repeated sessions. Better spatial specificity may come at the expense of signal strength, coverage, speed or tolerable exposure. Resolving those tradeoffs requires measurement and safety evidence. The supplied material does not establish a categorical absence of identified-neuron recording or control by focused ultrasound or hybrid acoustoelectric methods, nor does its discussion of optoacoustics establish the capabilities of acoustoelectric techniques.

current_state.text: Estrada and colleagues' perspective, published on 5 August 2025 in Nature Biomedical Engineering, volume 9, pages 1574–1590, identifies the skull as a substantial obstacle to transcranial light- and sound-based brain imaging. The supplied review had a subscription preview with the abstract, rather than the complete main article. The retained material discusses wave propagation, skull-induced distortions and compensatory strategies. It does not demonstrate cellular read and write or establish a fundamental resolution limit.

The research notes attribute a functional-ultrasound result to Rabut and colleagues in Science Translational Medicine on 29 May 2024, reporting approximately 200 μm resolution through a skull replacement rather than intact adult skull. However, the retained PubMed artifact available to the supplied review contains only a cookie notice. The study identity, numerical resolution and access configuration therefore remain unverified in this evidence package. This access failure is not evidence that the reported result is false. If confirmed as described, a hemodynamic imaging result at that spatial scale would still not, by itself, demonstrate individual-neuron spike recording.

Tang and colleagues' study, published on 1 May 2023, demonstrates noninvasive semantic reconstruction from BOLD fMRI and states that subject cooperation is required both to train and to apply the decoder. Its achievement is reconstruction of meaning from hemodynamic responses, rather than direct measurement of individual spikes. The study's reporting summary specifies 2.6 mm slice thickness and describes preprocessing consistent with two-second volume sampling. That sampling interval is an acquisition detail, not evidence of spike-level temporal resolution.

For the Tang study, the supplied review had a subscription preview of the main article and a complete reporting-summary document, not a complete main-paper extraction. A separate saved PDF was an unrelated language-model paper and contributes no neuroscience evidence; its misassociation does not invalidate the correctly identified study materials.

Kunz and colleagues' 2025 Cell inner-speech study examined four BrainGate2 participants with microelectrode arrays implanted in motor cortex. One participant's methods describe four 64-channel intracortical arrays placed in December 2023 in the left precentral gyrus. The signal-processing methods use threshold-crossing rates and spike-band power as estimates of local spiking activity; these measures should not automatically be equated with stable identification of every contributing neuron. This is an invasive recording result, and its discussion limits extrapolation to free-form thought decoding. The supplied manuscript extraction is truncated, although the reviewed passages directly support these points.

Evidence-scope synthesis: these dated sources establish relevant barriers and neighboring achievements, but the supplied bounded search record is empty. They do not establish a comprehensive field-wide absence of the proposed capability as of the review's 1 November 2026 reference date. Retrieval timestamps in November 2026 do not constitute a fresh literature assessment. The combined intact-skull cellular read-and-write capability is not demonstrated by the supplied evidence, while its present-day availability remains unassessed comprehensively.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: in awake adult humans with intact skulls, record simultaneous spikes from many individually tracked neurons, including neurons at depth, with enough stability to decode a simple ongoing behavior. Specify neuron count, anatomical depth, coverage, recording duration, spike-detection accuracy and cell-identity confidence before evaluating success. Behavior decoding should demonstrate functional usefulness, while independent validation must establish cellular resolution. These are proposed operational criteria, not published consensus standards.
completion_criteria.label: Simultaneous deep-neuron spike recordings decode behavior in awake adult humans

completion_criteria.text: Proposed write demonstration: prospectively choose an identified neuron or small group, alter its activity and verify the resulting neural change while quantifying unintended effects on surrounding cells. Establish read and write performance separately before demonstrating their combined use. The operative human capability must not require a cranial window, skull replacement or implanted electrode. A millimeter-scale hemodynamic map, even if useful for decoding or targeting, would not meet the cellular-spike criterion.
completion_criteria.label: Selected neurons are perturbed through intact skulls with quantified off-target effects

completion_criteria.text: Proposed validation: use suitable independent reference measurements in development settings where they are available, together with controls that test motion artifacts, signal mixing, reconstruction assumptions and stimulus artifacts. Report missed spikes, false detections, mistaken cell identities and off-target perturbations. Validation against an invasive reference in a separate development setting would support measurement accuracy; it would not substitute for demonstrating operation through intact adult human skull.
completion_criteria.label: Independent references and artifact controls validate reported cellular read-write accuracy

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and practical boundaries: replicate results across participants, sessions and independent teams, and report failures alongside successful cases. Define repeated-session safety endpoints, follow-up duration, exposure limits, tolerability and any required preparation or targeting agents. State the demonstrated depths, regions, cell types, neuron counts and task conditions. Finite tests can establish breadth within those conditions, not access to every neuron, every brain or every mental state. Clinical efficacy and routine scan-like deployment would require further demonstrations.
completion_criteria.label: Independent replication reports failures, safety endpoints and demonstrated operating limits

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — NEU-01, simultaneous spike-resolved recording from every neuron in one behaving mammalian brain: both concepts seek spike-level measurement. NEU-01 requires exhaustive whole-brain coverage; NEU-07 requires noninvasive access through intact adult human skull and adds selective write. Recording many neurons through skull would not establish recording from every neuron, and whole-brain recording in another preparation would not establish intact-skull human access.

Roster-based synthesis — NEU-02, routine synaptic-resolution connectomics of entire mammalian brains, and NEU-03, a prospective theory predicting circuit computation from connectivity: these address structural mapping and predictive interpretation, respectively. NEU-07 could supply activity and perturbation data to test circuit models, but cellular readout does not reveal every synapse or explain how connectivity generates computation.

Roster-based synthesis — NEU-04, content-faithful reading and writing of specific episodic memories: cellular access could provide an experimental interface for memory research, but identifying a particular episode and faithfully reading or changing its content are additional challenges. The earlier notes associated semantic and inner-speech decoding with NEU-04; the supplied roster defines NEU-04 specifically around episodic memory. Those language studies are useful comparators for measurement and interpretation, not demonstrations of the roster's memory capability.

Roster-based synthesis — NEU-05, target-specific regrowth of long axons in the adult mammalian central nervous system, and NEU-06, reconstruction of human cognitive circuits after neurons have been lost: NEU-07 could potentially measure surviving activity or test restored circuit function. Recording and perturbing cells would not itself regrow axons, replace lost neurons or reconstruct the information needed for recovered cognition.

Roster-based synthesis — NEU-08, a generative developmental code that builds a specified functional neural circuit, and NEU-09, cell-type-specific molecular access throughout the intact adult human brain: NEU-08 concerns constructing circuits, while NEU-09 concerns reaching cells according to molecular identity across the brain. Molecular access might support a future sensing or targeting strategy, but NEU-07 does not inherently provide cell-type specificity or whole-brain delivery. Conversely, molecular delivery alone would not demonstrate spike readout or selective control through skull.

Roster-based synthesis — NEU-10, a causal, measurement-grade account of conscious content: selective cellular perturbation could help test causal hypotheses about conscious experience. Establishing a causal account of content would still require theories, measurements and discriminating experiments beyond physical access to neurons.

Roster-based synthesis — NEU-11, reversible, circuit-specific reopening of critical-period plasticity in the adult brain, and NEU-12, completing sleep's necessary brain functions without a normal sleep period: NEU-07 could potentially monitor or perturb circuits during plasticity and sleep research. Selective stimulation does not establish reversible control of a plasticity program, an adequate account of sleep's functions or the ability to replace those functions.

unresolved_issues: The approximately 200 μm Rabut functional-ultrasound result, publication details and skull-replacement configuration require verification from scientific content rather than the retained cookie notice.
A bounded, current literature assessment is needed to determine whether any approach has demonstrated the combined capability, or either component, through intact adult human skull.

The specific inverse-problem, scalp electromagnetic, focused-ultrasound and acoustoelectric claims require additional inspected evidence; optoacoustic discussion cannot resolve acoustoelectric claims.
No supplied evidence establishes whether the combined capability is physically achievable, an ultimate cellular-resolution ceiling or a defensible development timeline.
Neuron count, depth, coverage, tracking duration, spike accuracy, write selectivity and safety endpoints remain proposed protocol specifications without numerical thresholds.
The supplied access and extraction limits leave portions of the underlying literature unassessed; no resolution is inferred from unavailable text.

brief.title: Reading and changing brain cells without surgery
possible: A person could stay awake, with their skull intact, while researchers followed the electrical pulses of many individual brain cells, including deep ones. Researchers could also selectively change the activity of a chosen cell or small group without surgery or implants.
why: Human neuroscience could connect the activity of identified cells to behavior, then test cause and effect by changing those cells and watching what happens.
Researchers could follow how brain circuits change during learning and disease. This access could also support the development of treatments aimed at particular circuits.

sources.who: Jerry Tang, Amanda LeBel, Shailee Jain and Alexander G. Huth
sources.showed: They reconstructed language meaning using functional magnetic resonance imaging, a scan that tracks blood-flow changes. Successful decoding required the person's cooperation.
sources.quote: We tested the decoder across cortex and found that continuous language can be separately decoded from multiple regions.
sources.cited_for: Language meaning can be reconstructed from brain signals without surgery.
sources.not_established: The scans did not identify individual brain cells or measure their electrical pulses.

sources.who: Erin M. Kunz, Benyamin Abramovich Krasa and colleagues
sources.showed: They decoded imagined sentences as they occurred using implanted electrodes in four participants. Their recordings combined signals from groups of cells.
sources.quote: Using multi-unit recordings from four participants, we found that inner speech is robustly represented in motor cortex, and that imagined sentences can be decoded in real-time.
sources.cited_for: Implanted electrodes can capture signals useful for decoding imagined speech.
sources.not_established: The work required implants and did not establish stable tracking of individual cells or accurate sentence decoding during free-form thought.

sources.who: Héctor Estrada, Thomas Deffieux, Justine Robin, Mickaël Tanter and Daniel Razansky
sources.showed: Their perspective explains how skull bone distorts light and sound used for brain imaging. It reviews efforts to model and compensate for those distortions.
sources.cited_for: The skull poses a substantial physical obstacle to imaging with light and sound.
sources.not_established: The perspective neither demonstrates access to individual cells nor establishes an ultimate limit on resolution.

sources.showed: They mapped task-related brain activity with ultrasound through a plastic skull replacement in one awake person. Ultrasound here tracks blood-flow changes.
sources.quote: We showed that fUSI could record brain activity in an awake human outside of the operating room.
sources.cited_for: A skull replacement can permit ultrasound imaging of brain activity outside an operating room.
sources.not_established: The work did not operate through an intact adult skull or record individual cells' electrical pulses.

shown: The demonstrated capabilities remain separate: Tang and colleagues reconstructed meaning without surgery; Kunz and colleagues decoded imagined speech with implants; Rabut and colleagues mapped activity through a skull replacement. None of these studies demonstrated both recording and selective control of individual cells through an intact adult human skull.
missing: A system must recover electrical pulses from many individually tracked cells through an intact adult skull, including at depth.
A separate targeting capability must change chosen cells' activity while measuring unintended changes in other cells.
Recording and control must work together over useful brain areas and repeated sessions, with measured safety and accuracy.

milestones.label: Deep brain cells tracked during behavior
milestones.explanation: An awake adult with an intact skull would have to yield simultaneous, stable recordings of many individual cells, including deep ones, sufficient to decode behavior. This would establish useful cellular recording.

milestones.label: Chosen cells changed with unintended effects measured
milestones.explanation: A system would have to change a chosen cell or small group's activity through an intact skull and measure effects on surrounding cells. This would establish selective control separately from recording.

milestones.label: Independent measurements confirm recording and control accuracy
milestones.explanation: Independent reference measurements and controls would have to quantify recording errors, mistaken cell identities and unintended stimulation while testing interference. This would distinguish cellular access from misleading signals.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce results and define safe operating limits
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to repeat results across people and sessions, reporting failures, repeated-use safety and operating limits. This would establish reliability and the conditions under which the capability works.

uncertain: It remains unknown whether combined recording and selective control of individual cells through an intact adult skull is physically achievable.
Success thresholds remain unsettled for cell count, depth, coverage, tracking duration, accuracy, selectivity and safety.
Greater precision may trade off against signal strength, coverage, speed or tolerable exposure.

page.title: Noninvasive single-neuron recording and stimulation
page.definition: A system records the electrical spikes of individual neurons and selectively changes a chosen neuron's firing in an awake adult human through an intact skull. Neither function requires cranial surgery, skull modification, an implanted interface or an injected neural transducer.

goal.need: Tang et al. reported language reconstruction from blood-oxygenation imaging in 3 adults after 16 h of listening each on 1 May 2023. Kunz et al. reported inner-speech decoding from multi-unit recordings in 4 participants on 14 August 2025. Rabut et al. reported 200 μm functional ultrasound imaging through a skull replacement in 1 adult on 29 May 2024. Cellular recording and selective stimulation without surgery would permit observing identified neurons and testing their causal contributions to behavior.

statements.body: NIH Advisory Committee to the Director, BRAIN Working Group
statements.quote: expand our ability to detect activity non‐invasively in the human brain.
statements.context: BRAIN 2025, Section 3g-iii, identifies this goal under human neuroimaging and describes an imaging modality with cellular spatial and temporal resolution.

statements.quote: The interface must be bidirectional and will integrate technology for both neural recording (read out) and neural stimulation (write in).
statements.context: The N3 solicitation distinguishes a fully external, ensemble-resolution track from a single-neuron track permitting nonsurgically delivered internal transducers.

completion.title: One system records and selectively stimulates an identified neuron through an awake adult human's intact skull.
completion.criterion: In at least 1 awake adult human, one system records an identified neuron's spike times and selectively changes that neuron's firing through the intact, unmodified skull. The demonstration establishes neuronal attribution, distinguishes the target from neighboring cells and measures unintended responses. Neither function requires cranial surgery, an implanted interface or an injected neural transducer. This is a first-demonstration test, without additional minimum cell count, depth, duration or accuracy requirements.
completion.set_by: Atlas; no external completion test located for this combined capability.
completion.basis: Searches of NIH BRAIN and DARPA N3 documents, FDA neurological-device guidance, IEEE.org and ClinicalTrials.gov found no completion test for combined noninvasive single-neuron human recording and stimulation. NIH explicitly declines to set milestones for the human imaging goal. N3 permits internal transducers for its single-neuron target. The Atlas therefore uses a first demonstration of both cellular functions together, without importing ensemble-resolution thresholds.

milestones.title: Neural populations are optically recorded and stimulated at cellular resolution in vivo.
milestones.criterion: Simultaneously image neural populations and deliver individually targeted optical stimulation at cellular resolution in vivo. Packer et al., published on 22 December 2014, stimulated 10 selected neurons while imaging them and 290 surrounding neurons at 30 Hz in 3 mice. Their preparation used genetically encoded proteins and cranial windows; calcium fluorescence supplied the activity readout.
milestones.set_by: NIH BRAIN Working Group, BRAIN 2025, Section 3g-ii, integrated optical recording and perturbation milestone.
milestones.threshold_quote: simultaneous optical imaging and optogenetic stimulation of neural populations at cellular resolution;

milestones.title: Transcranial recording and stimulation components operate for ≥2 h with ≥95% ground-truth accuracy.
milestones.criterion: Read and write components work through skull or a skull-like medium for ≥2 h, with spatial resolution <1 mm³, temporal resolution <10 ms and DARPA's ≥95% ground-truth accuracy metric. This is an ensemble-resolution bench test; it does not establish individual-neuron access.
milestones.set_by: DARPA N3, HR001118S0029, TA1 Phase I; numerical thresholds appear in Table 1.

milestones.title: An external interface records and stimulates ≥16 channels each in a mammal with <100 ms loop latency.
milestones.criterion: An integrated interface in a higher-order mammal or human provides ≥16 read and ≥16 write channels per 16 mm³, <100 ms closed-loop latency, ≥3 control degrees of freedom and ≥3 somatosensory categories, with task-useful sensory feedback. Device volume is ≤125 cm³; Phase I metrics persist. Table 1 also limits tissue heating to a 1° rise but does not specify its temperature unit. This remains an ensemble-resolution test.
milestones.set_by: DARPA N3, HR001118S0029, TA1 Phase II; numerical thresholds appear in Table 1.

milestones.title: An individual neuron's spike times are recorded through an awake adult human's intact skull.
milestones.criterion: In at least 1 awake adult human, externally record spike times attributable to an individually identified neuron through the intact, unmodified skull, distinguishing its signal from neighboring cells. Operation requires no cranial surgery, implanted interface or injected neural transducer. This Atlas component test has no externally established minimum depth, duration or accuracy.
milestones.set_by: Atlas; no matching human recording endpoint located in roadmap, regulator, standards or trial-registry searches.

milestones.title: A chosen neuron's firing is selectively changed through an awake adult human's intact skull.
milestones.criterion: In at least 1 awake adult human, selectively change a prospectively chosen neuron's firing through the intact, unmodified skull without cranial surgery, an implanted interface or injected neural transducer; measure neighboring-cell responses. Dickey et al., published on 2 November 2026, measured responses of 185 neurons in 4 patients using implanted electrodes: magnetic stimulation modulated 46%. This demonstrates cellular responses without establishing individual-cell targeting.
milestones.set_by: Atlas; no matching human single-cell targeting endpoint located in roadmap, regulator, standards or trial-registry searches.

not_found: No external test specifying combined noninvasive single-neuron recording and selective stimulation through an intact adult human skull was located.
No demonstration satisfying the combined human completion test was located.
No publication verifying all N3 TA1 Phase I or Phase II performance metrics together was located.
The publisher full texts of the Kunz inner-speech paper and Estrada skull-imaging perspective could not be opened; the Kunz abstract was accessible on a coauthor's laboratory website.
N3 Table 1 does not specify a temperature unit for its 1° tissue-heating limit.

results.finding: Functional ultrasound imaged brain activity in 1 awake adult human at 200 μm resolution.
results.detail: The patient had a surgically implanted cranial window. The reported functional imaging did not establish spike times attributable to an individual neuron or distinguish its signal from neighboring cells.
results.quote: Our proof-of-principle study shows that fUSI can be used as a high-resolution (200 μm) functional imaging modality for measuring adult human brain activity through an acoustically transparent cranial window.

results.finding: In 6 mice, individually targeted optical stimulation increased activity in 346 neurons in one example animal.
results.detail: Across 16 sessions, researchers used holographic stimulation and cellular-resolution calcium imaging in vivo. The example targeted 408 neurons; non-targeted cells also showed activity changes.
results.quote:
In one example animal under
these conditions, we could simultaneously increase the activity
of 346 neurons for a 408-target hologram ( Figures 8 D and 8E;
Wilcoxon rank-sum test, one-tailed p < 0.025).

results.finding: In behaving mice, 18 pairs of CA1 neurons were optically stimulated and imaged at cellular resolution.
results.detail: The study used genetically encoded voltage indicators and optogenetic actuators. The preparation included cranial windows.
results.quote: In head-fixed mice running on a spherical treadmill, targeting optogenetic stimulation to single cells while simultaneously imaging surrounding cells revealed minimal direct stimulation of surrounding cells

results.finding: In mouse cortex, targeted neurons were simultaneously stimulated and calcium-imaged at 600 µm depth across 2 fields of view; mouse count not stated.
results.detail: The transgenic mice co-expressed ChRmine and GCaMP6m. The authors report simultaneous stimulation of two neurons with single-cell spatial resolution; calcium fluorescence was the activity readout.
